A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same U-ViT3D-Mixer research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, are readable and support matching across revisions and relocations.

before.justification: V1 reports original shape and albedo benchmark results, architectural and motion ablations, ambiguity experiments, and an appendix probing experiment.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, Stanford-ORB evaluation, motion-generalization tests, an IID evaluation-protocol comparison, and inference-resource measurements.

M1.justification: The joint U-ViT3D-Mixer architecture, local spatial and temporal attention, channel mixers, attribute loss weights and DDIM inference remain unchanged. Appendix A.4's temporal-consistency guidance already appears in v1; its rewritten explanation does not establish a new procedure.

E1.justification: V2 adds Stanford-ORB evaluation with moving-camera observations and systematic tests of random-axis rotations and random translations. These substantially broaden the tested motion and observation conditions. The synthetic training coverage, DiLiGent and MIT-Intrinsic benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Marigold–Albedo to the MIT-Intrinsic comparison. Figure 8 adds DiffusionRenderer to the real-video comparison, which previously compared against RGB-X alone. Adding a directly relevant video-based inverse-rendering comparator substantially strengthens comparison on the central motion task.

E3.justification: Existing training and Tables 1–2 protocols remain. New protocols include a controlled 174-object comparison across three motion conditions, six-scene Stanford-ORB evaluation using three nearby views, IID mean-prediction versus best-three evaluation with LPIPS, and FP32 resource profiling on one A100. These substantially expand evaluation design without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: New analyses test generalization to unfamiliar rotations and translations (A.7), sensitivity to IID prediction aggregation (A.5), and computational resource requirements (A.10). The original architectural and motion ablations, normal-estimation probing, and temporal-consistency discussion are retained, including relocated material.

E5.justification: Both versions retain ten stochastic predictions for the principal benchmark evaluations and 100-sample ambiguity visualizations. Neither adds training-seed replication, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new IID aggregation comparison concerns evaluation accuracy rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All retained entries in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. V2 adds Marigold–Albedo results of 0.72 SSIM, 0.11 RMSE and 19.86 PSNR, plus Tables 3–7. For example, Table 6 reports mean angular errors of 12.267, 15.062 and 16.652 for vertical-axis rotation, random rotation and random translation. Figure 8 expands qualitative comparisons, and Figure 4 replaces several predicted normal maps. These are additional or revised results, without evidence of improved scores on the retained evaluations.

T1.justification: The formal imaging assumptions, diffusion equations and appendix reflectance formulation remain substantively unchanged, including Equations 1–14. Explicitly including the frame dimension in material-map notation clarifies the existing time-varying representation. No new theorem, proof or derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: joint generative shape-and-material estimation, multimodal interpretations of ambiguous static inputs, and disambiguation through differential motion. Revised wording and additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: V1 emphasizes restricted rotation axes and isolated objects. V2 explains generalization through local attention and training-shape diversity, recognizes multiple objects sharing rigid motion, and specifies failures involving deformation, distinct motions, transparency and translucency. It also explicitly identifies foreground segmentation as a requirement. These materially revise the stated applicability boundaries and mechanism explanations.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents foreground segmentation and background masking, describes multi-object and self-occluding training assets, and supplies FP32 model-size and GPU-memory information. It also provides a concrete project-page URL where v1 only mentions a website. The detailed architecture hyperparameters and training recipe remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to DiffusionRenderer, Stable Video Diffusion, the newer Marigold work and Stanford-ORB. It contrasts joint inference with DiffusionRenderer's attribute-conditioned outputs and removes Section 4.2's assertion that no joint video baselines exist. The broader positioning remains stable; most appendix references are relocated rather than newly added.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten and reordered to present ambiguity before motion. Explanatory passages and the conclusion are revised, limitations move into Section 4.3, and the appendix is reorganized, including moving the probing experiment from A.6 to A.2 and separating appendix references. This is substantial editorial restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V1's combined Figure 7 becomes a retained ambiguity figure and an expanded real-video comparison in v2's Figure 8. V2 adds five tables, enlarges the main tables, refreshes some Figure 4 samples, and relocates the probing figure. The original appendix ablation figure survives as Figure 10. These substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central motion-based perception claim through a relevant video comparator, quantitative captured camera-motion evaluation, and controlled unfamiliar-motion tests. These address v1's explicitly unresolved motion-generalization limitations. The IID protocol check and more precise applicability boundaries further improve transparency. The new evidence is mixed—Stanford-ORB shape error beats Marigold-e2e-ft on only two of six objects—and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but the expanded validation provides a substantial overall quality gain.
